parsed.citation_summary: Milner and Judson (abstract only) study electoral institutions and public expenditure in OECD and Latin American countries. The paper presents a theoretical model predicting that proportional systems lead to more transfer/public good spending while majoritarian systems lead to more goods/services purchases. The abstract claims 'considerable support' for predictions but provides no quantitative effect estimates, confidence intervals, or standard errors. No specific empirical methodology is described in the available abstract.

mechanisms.description: Voters anticipate government policy-making under different electoral systems and have incentives to elect representatives whose preferences align with the spending patterns facilitated by those systems. Proportional systems facilitate transfer and public good spending preferences, while majoritarian systems facilitate goods and services purchasing preferences.
mechanisms.theoretical_framework: Theoretical model of electoral institutions and public expenditure allocation

parsed.methodology: The abstract mentions defining 'rigorous measures of proportionality' for empirical investigation, but no specific econometric methodology is described. The paper appears to use cross-country comparative analysis with measures of electoral proportionality, but the identification strategy (e.g., instrumental variables, panel fixed effects, difference-in-differences) is not specified in the available abstract.
